papers.title: Early potassium response to mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist therapy and cardiovascular outcomes in primary aldosteronism: a landmark cohort study
papers.abstract: Background Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs) are standard therapy for primary aldosteronism (PA). Serum potassium is measured in nearly every treated patient, but the long-term prognostic value of potassium attained early after initiation is undefined. Methods In the TriNetX Research Network, we identified adults with PA newly initiating spironolactone or eplerenone in 2000-2025, without prior adrenalectomy (n=4,169; 180-day landmark design). Achieved potassium (last value on days 14-180) was categorised as <4.0, 4.0-<4.5, 4.5-<5.0 and [≥]5.0 mmol/L, and its change from baseline in tertiles, using cause-specific Cox and Fine-Gray models. The primary outcome was a composite of myocardial infarction, stroke or death; incident heart failure was co-primary. Findings Over a median 3.0 years, 623 composite events occurred. Estimated risk was lowest at 4.5-<5.0 mmol/L (adjusted hazard ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.52-0.83, versus <4.0 mmol/L), lower than the 4.0-<4.5 mmol/L band, and not different from [≥]5.0 mmol/L. A larger rise in potassium was associated with lower risk. A similar pattern was seen for incident heart failure (0.54, 0.36-0.80; 248 events). Potassium below the 3.6 mmol/L consensus threshold for hypokalaemia carried no significantly higher risk (1.22, 0.96-1.56). The change in potassium correlated weakly with the change in renin (rho = 0.15). Interpretation In MRA-treated PA, cardiovascular and heart-failure risk was lowest at an early achieved potassium of 4.5-<5.0 mmol/L, well above the 3.6 mmol/L accepted by consensus criteria as correction of hypokalaemia; correction alone may therefore be an insufficient treatment target. Whether titrating therapy towards this band improves outcomes requires prospective evaluation.

papers.title: Wavelet-derived indices of cardiac vagal and vasomotor oscillations as a new tool to better understand autonomic imbalance in post-COVID-19 dysautonomia
papers.abstract: Background: When aiming to quantify autonomic imbalance, conventional heart rate variability (HRV) analysis generally reduces each posture to a single spectral value derived from interbeat intervals (IBI) alone. This analysis based only in IBI obscures transient events during blood pressure changes. We propose two wavelet-derived indices that quantify cardiac vagal and vasomotor sympathetic oscillations separately and over time. Since autonomic imbalance is directly related to baroreflex sensitivity (BRS), we evaluated them against an estimate of baroreflex sensitivity in post-COVID-19 patients. Methods: In this study, 121 participants (32 healthy controls and 89 patients with persistent post-COVID-19 autonomic symptoms) underwent an active standing test with continuous finger blood pressure. The continuous wavelet transform with generalized Morse wavelets yielded time-varying high-frequency power of IBI and low-frequency power of systolic blood pressure (SBP). Two new indices were proposed: Index I combined the magnitude and variability of HF IBI power (aimed to quantify parasympathetic activity), and the index J combined LF SBP power with the rate of its transient elevations (bursts), which aims to quantify sympathetic vasomotor activity; J/I was their ratio. Indices were computed for supine and orthostatic periods and compared with conventional HRV and BRS measurements. Results: Index I correlated strongly with HF power of IBI and was lower in all patient subgroups than in controls, Index J had only a weak relation with LF power of IBI. On standing, J increased most in the subgroups with the worst baroreflex function. Orthostatic J/I was higher than in controls in all three subgroups, while LF/HF showed no differences. J/I was inversely correlated with BRS, most strongly when standing, and more strongly than LF/HF also. Adding J to I raised the cross-validated variance explained in orthostatic BRS substantially. In one example patient, a window during symptoms showed vasomotor oscillations that were hidden in the posture average. Conclusions: Wavelet-derived indices from routine beat-to-beat recordings separate cardiac vagal modulation from sympathetic vasomotor oscillations and their transients. J/I correlates with BRS impairment more closely than LF/HF, providing a potential alternative estimate of autonomic balance, and its time-resolved visual output allows analysis of clinically relevant windows within a posture. The new proposed variables allowed an evaluation of autonomic imbalance that could be applied to different pathologies. Keywords: continuous wavelet transform; heart rate variability; blood pressure variability; baroreflex sensitivity; Mayer waves; dysautonomia; long COVID; active standing test; autonomic imbalance.

papers.title: Cardiorespiratory Limits Exist in HFpEF Independent of Age and BMI
papers.abstract: Background: Heart-failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is a clinical syndrome marked by exercise intolerance associated with impairments in cardiac and respiratory performance. HFpEF is associated with age and weight; however, it remains unclear whether cardiorespiratory limitations exist independent of these comorbidities. Hypothesis: Independent of age and BMI, there are cardiorespiratory limitations inherent to the HFpEF syndrome that have yet to be fully elicited. Methods: A patient cohort with a clinical diagnosis of HFpEF (HFpEF; N = 38) and counterparts without identifiable cardiopulmonary disease (control; N = 21) underwent phenotyping with echocardiography and cardiopulmonary exercise testing with invasive hemodynamic monitoring. Results: Study cohorts were similar in age, BMI and height (p=NS for all metrics). Body-surface area (BSA) (2.1 m2 v 1.9 m2, p < 0.05), atrial fibrillation prevalence (50 v 14%, p < 0.05), and average E/e (11.5 v 9.5, p < 0.05) were elevated within the HFpEF cohort. Peak VO2 (14.1 v 19.1 mL/Kg/min, p < 0.001) was also diminished among those with HFpEF. Resting (17.1 v 11.4mmHg, p < 0.001) and exercise wedge pressures (29.3 v 16.7mmHg, p < 0.001) were elevated whereas stroke volume (93.3 v 110.4 mL, p < 0.05) and cardiac output (Direct Fick; 8.0 v 9.8, p < 0.05) during exercise were diminished in HFpEF patients. FVC, FVC%, FEV1 and FEV1% were also significantly diminished in the HFpEF cohort. Conclusions: Cardiorespiratory limitations exist as a feature of the HFpEF syndrome, independent of age and BMI. BSA remained associated with HFpEF in keeping with adiposity as a feature of pathophysiology.

papers.title: B-cell involvement supports anti-CD20 therapy in paediatric rheumatic heart disease: Proof of concept and initial safety
papers.abstract: Rheumatic heart disease (RHD) remains a major cause of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, yet no therapy targets its underlying autoimmune mechanisms. We combined transcriptomic analyses of rheumatic mitral valves tissues with a translational approach. Using a panel of 750 mRNAs, we found a marked upregulation of B-cell-related pathways, including CD20-associated and multiple immunoglobulin genes, supporting a pathogenic role of B cells in RHD. We therefore evaluated an anti-CD20 B-cell depleting monoclonal antibody (Rituximab), in a feasibility study in children with RHD, in Dakar, Senegal. Treatment was well tolerated, and in the following RCT first year preliminary safety analysis asked by the ethical committee, children who received rituximab showed a decrease in anti-streptolysin O titers and clinical improvement compared to controls. This proof-of-concept reveals B cells as a therapeutic target and suggests that an anti-CD20 agent may represent a potential disease-modifying therapy for RHD.

papers.title: Reconstructing the range-normalized terminal QRS from V1 and V6 using the time-embedded 3D ECG
papers.abstract: Objective. Can a fixed V1/V6 projection of the time-embedded 3D ECG estimate the final 40 ms of V2-V5 more accurately than a fitted single lead? Methods. We used simultaneous recordings from the Lobachevsky University Electrocardiography Database (LUDB), with cardiologist-annotated QRS complexes in all six chest leads. We fitted both models in 118 patients and tested them in 80 others. Root mean squared error (RMSE) is expressed in percentage points (pp) of the target lead's 10-second amplitude range. Results. In 733 test beats, patient-weighted terminal RMSE fell from 12.58 to 10.64 pp (difference 1.94 pp, 95% bootstrap confidence interval 1.30 to 2.55). Reductions were 3.23, 2.85 and 1.35 pp in V3, V4 and V5. In V2 the difference was 0.35 pp (95% interval -0.35 to 1.05). In 702 matched beats from 77 patients, the overall advantage was 2.22 pp at the automatic V1/V6 end and 1.92 pp at the annotated target end. Of 1,498 beat-lead pairs with whole-QRS correlation of at least 0.95, 28.84% still had terminal RMSE of at least 10 pp. Conclusions. A fixed V1/V6 projection improved offline estimates of relative terminal amplitude in V3-V5 without fitting the target lead in the new patient. The gain was largest in V3 and V4 and uncertain in V2. Whether a reconstructed trace preserves a clinically recognizable notch or slur remains untested.

papers.title: Distinct circulating proteomic patterns associated with thoracic aortic diameter and stiffness: A proteome-wide study in the UK Biobank
papers.abstract: Background: Thoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA) is characterized by abnormal dilation and functional remodelling of the thoracic aorta. Current detection and surveillance rely largely on imaging, limiting population-wide risk stratification. Circulating proteins may provide biological insight into aortic remodelling and support future biomarker development. We aimed to identify circulating proteomic patterns associated with imaging-derived thoracic aortic diameter and aortic stiffness in a large population-based cohort. Methods: A proteome-wide association study was conducted in 6773 UK Biobank participants with available plasma proteomic and cardiac imaging data. A combined thoracic aortic diameter was derived from taking the maximum of standardized ascending and descending measurements, while stiffness was derived using a pressure-free index of aortic wall properties. Associations with 2920 circulating proteins were evaluated using multivariable linear regression with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Functional enrichment analysis was performed using the complete ranked protein list across Hallmark, curated, and Gene Ontology Biological Process collections. Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed as a secondary analysis to explore shared and divergent variation between the two phenotypes. Results: In age- and sex-adjusted analyses, 358 proteins were associated with aortic diameter and 60 with stiffness after FDR correction. Sequential adjustment materially altered these associations; in the primary fully adjusted models, 417 proteins were associated with diameter and six with stiffness. Functional enrichment analyses highlighted complement/coagulation, extracellular matrix organization, and contractile pathways associated with aortic diameter. In contrast, although only a few individual proteins were associated with stiffness, rank-based pathway analysis across the full proteome identified a distinct enrichment pattern involving cytokine signalling, protein processing, and intracellular transport. Aortic diameter and stiffness were only modestly correlated (r = 0.21). Secondary PCA showed that the first principal component (PC1) largely overlapped with the diameter-associated profile, with 310 of 370 PC1-associated proteins also associated with diameter. Four proteins (REN, BCAN, GGH and THY1) were associated with both diameter and stiffness in addition to being associated with PC1. Conclusion: Circulating proteomic profiling identified markedly different and minimally overlapping molecular patterns associated with thoracic aortic diameter and stiffness. Structural dilation was primarily linked to complement/coagulation, extracellular matrix, and contractile pathways, whereas stiffness reflected a smaller, more distinct aspect of aortic remodelling involving cytokine signalling and cellular transport processes. The four shared proteins across both phenotypes (REN, BCAN, GGH and THY1) represent candidates for further biomarker and causal investigation.

papers.title: Sleep Irregularity and Risk of Incident Hypertension in the UK Biobank
papers.abstract: BackgroundIrregular sleep patterns are common and have been associated with higher cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk. Hypertension is the leading modifiable cause of CVD, but evidence linking irregular sleep to hypertension is inconsistent. The objective of this study was to quantify associations between irregular sleep and incident hypertension. MethodsWe conducted a prospective cohort study among 55,572 UK Biobank participants without hypertension or anti-hypertensive medication use who provided [≥]5 valid days of accelerometry in 2013- 2015 (60% women, mean age 61 years). We measured sleep regularity using the intra-individual standard deviation (SD) of sleep duration and the sleep regularity index (SRI), a measure of the similarity of sleep-wake patterns from one day to the next. Cox proportional hazards models estimated adjusted hazard ratios (HR) for incident hypertension, identified through linked health records, by levels of sleep regularity adjusting for demographic, socioeconomic, and lifestyle factors as well as employment schedule. We also evaluated differences by demographic, clinical, and sleep-related (defined by duration, efficiency, timing, and sleep disorders) subgroups, and interaction with genetic susceptibility to hypertension. ResultsDuring 7.9 years of follow-up, 5,713 participants developed hypertension. Participants with sleep duration SD >90 minutes had an 18% higher risk of incident hypertension compared to those with sleep duration SD [≤]30 minutes (HR: 1.18; 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.06, 1.31). Similarly, participants in the lowest SRI quintile had a 40% higher risk than those in the highest SRI quintile (HR: 1.40; 95% CI: 1.29, 1.52). These associations were generally consistent across demographic, health, and sleep-defined subgroups. Sleep irregularity and genetic susceptibility contributed independently to hypertension risk, without evidence of interaction. ConclusionsIrregular sleep patterns were associated with higher incident hypertension risk independent of established risk factors and genetic susceptibility. Maintaining regular sleep schedules may represent a modifiable behavioral target for hypertension prevention. Clinical PerspectiveO_ST_ABSWhat is new?C_ST_ABSO_LIIn this large prospective study using objectively measured sleep from wrist accelerometry, greater overall variability in sleep duration and more irregular day-to-day sleep-wake patterns were independently associated with higher risk of incident hypertension. C_LIO_LIAssociations were robust to adjustment for potential confounding by demographic, socioeconomic, clinical, and lifestyle factors and were generally consistent across demographic, clinical, and sleep-defined subgroups. C_LIO_LISleep regularity and genetic susceptibility to hypertension were independently associated with hypertension risk, with no evidence that inherited risk modified the association between irregular sleep and incident hypertension. C_LI What are the clinical implications?O_LIMaintaining consistent sleep schedules may represent an important modifiable behavioral target for hypertension prevention alongside established lifestyle recommendations. C_LIO_LIThe association between irregular sleep and hypertension was observed regardless of genetic susceptibility, suggesting that improving sleep regularity may benefit individuals across the spectrum of inherited hypertension risk. C_LIO_LIThese findings support future randomized clinical trials to determine whether interventions that improve sleep regularity can reduce blood pressure and prevent hypertension. C_LI

papers.title: Feasibility of AI-Guided Handheld Echocardiography for Rheumatic Heart Disease Screening by Non-Cardiologists in Rural Nepal: A Mixed-Methods Diagnostic Accuracy Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundRheumatic heart disease remains a major cause of preventable morbidity and mortality in rural Nepal, where access to cardiovascular specialists and echocardiography is limited. We evaluated the diagnostic accuracy and feasibility of AI-guided echocardiography performed by nurse practitioners for community-based RHD screening. MethodsWe conducted a triangulation mixed-methods study (QUAN > qual) combining a paired cross-sectional diagnostic accuracy study with semi-structured interviews during community screening camps in Damak, Nepal, in November 2025. Nurse practitioners performed AI-guided handheld echocardiography using EchoNous Kosmos Plus devices, with cardiologist overread serving as the comparator. Diagnostic performance was assessed using sensitivity, specificity, and kappa. Interviews were analyzed thematically. ResultsOf 90 participants enrolled, 76 were included in the final analysis. Mean age was 50.8 years, 57.8% were male, and 42.2% had undergone prior cardiac evaluation. Detection of any valvular lesion demonstrated 95.8% sensitivity and 100% specificity, with near-perfect agreement with cardiologist interpretation ({kappa}=0.97). Lesion-specific performance included mitral regurgitation sensitivity 66.7% and specificity 97.3% ({kappa}=0.55), mitral stenosis sensitivity 100% and specificity 97.2% ({kappa}=0.81), aortic regurgitation sensitivity 90.9% and specificity 96.9% ({kappa}=0.84), and tricuspid regurgitation sensitivity and specificity of 100% ({kappa}=1.00). Mean scan duration was 5.8 minutes. Portability, AI-assisted acquisition, and remote review facilitated implementation, while training needs, workflow constraints, and technical issues were barriers. ConclusionsAI-guided handheld echocardiography performed by nurses demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy and feasibility for rural RHD screening. AI-assisted task-shifting may expand access to early RHD detection in underserved settings.

papers.title: Mental Stress-Induced Peripheral Microvascular Dysfunction and Cardiovascular Events after a Premature Myocardial Infarction: A Prospective Cohort Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundImpaired macrovascular function during acute mental stress predicts adverse events in coronary artery disease, but microvascular stress responses are less understood. Because psychosocial stress and coronary microvascular dysfunction are more common in women, sex differences also warrant study. MethodsWe studied individuals aged 18-60 years within 8 months of a myocardial infarction (MI) who underwent a standardized mental stress challenge and were followed for cardiovascular events. We measured peripheral microvascular function with the reactive hyperemia index (RHI) before and after stress; abnormal RHI was defined as [≤]1.67. We also measured brachial flow-mediated vasodilation (FMD), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and myocardial ischemia. The primary endpoint was a composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, stroke, or heart failure hospitalization; a secondary endpoint included recurrent events. Cox regression examined stress-induced RHI decline, adjusting for pre-stress RHI and demographic, clinical, and psychological factors. ResultsAmong 487 participants (mean age 51 years; 43% women), 89 first and 90 recurrent events occurred over a median 34 months. Women had lower RHI than men before and after stress, and a larger stress-induced decline. Each standard deviation stress-induced RHI decline was associated with 36% higher risk of first events (hazard ratio [HR], 1.36, 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.01, 1.82) and 44% higher risk of cumulative events (HR, 1.44, 95% CI, 1.04, 2.00), with no significant sex interaction. Abnormal post-stress RHI conferred adjusted HRs of 2.59 (95% CI, 1.13, 5.92) in women and 2.09 (95% CI, 1.11, 3.93) in men; abnormal pre-stress RHI was not predictive (HR, 1.12, 95% CI, 0.71, 1.76). IL-6 and FMD changes and stress-induced ischemia were related to RHI decline but did not explain its association with outcome. ConclusionsMicrovascular dysfunction with mental stress is more prevalent in women, and signals an elevated cardiovascular risk after MI in both women and men. What is already known on this topicMacrovascular dysfunction in response to acute mental stress has been related to increased risk of recurrent events in people with coronary artery disease. However, less is known about microvascular responses to stress. What this study addsA decline in microvascular function with mental stress is an independent predictor of subsequent cardiovascular events after a myocardial infarction (MI), and a stronger predictor than pre-stress microvascular function alone. Women have worse resting microvascular function and a more adverse microvascular response to stress. How this study might affect research, practice or policyMicrovascular dysfunction may represent an important pathway linking psychological stress to adverse cardiovascular outcomes in people with MI. The microvascular response to stress should be evaluated as a potentially modifiable marker of cardiovascular risk and intervention studies should determine whether targeting stress-related microvascular dysfunction can reduce cardiovascular risk in this population.

papers.title: Oxygen Uptake Efficiency Slope (OUES) and Mortality in Chronic Heart Failure: Comparisons of Absolute and Percent-predicted Values across Different Equations
papers.abstract: AimThe oxygen uptake efficiency slope (OUES) is a prognostic indicator obtained from cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPX) in chronic heart failure (CHF) patients. Although various equations exist for calculating predicted OUES, it remains unclear whether absolute or percent-predicted values offer a more accurate prognostic assessment. To investigate and compare mortality prediction in CHF patients using the OUES absolute values or the percent-predicted approach, incorporating the equations of Hollenberg, Buys, and Milani. MethodsRetrospective cohort study involving CHF patients evaluated at a tertiary university hospital between July 2013 and July 2023. All patients underwent maximal CPX and were followed in a specialized outpatient clinic. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality. To compare the prognostic accuracy between different approaches, we performed receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis and Cox proportional hazards regression. ResultsA total of 1.180 patients were included, 57% male, with a mean age of 55 {+/-} 12 years. The median follow-up was 5.0 years (IQR 3.0 to 7.2 years), resulting in 147 deaths (12.5%). The area under de curve (AUC) was 0.71 to 0.72 for males, and 0.60 to 0.63 for females, without statistical difference in the AUC between absolute and percent-predicted OUES. Different cut-offs were identified for each sex for predicting mortality and all OUES metrics remained independent predictors in multivariate models using sex and age. ConclusionsOUES, in both absolute and percent-predicted forms, demonstrated similar accuracy in predicting mortality in CHF, with sex-specific cut-offs influencing clinical assessment. Condensed AbstractO_ST_ABSAimC_ST_ABSCompare absolute and percent-predicted OUES (Hollenberg, Buys, Milani) for mortality prediction in chronic heart failure. MethodsRetrospective cohort of 1,180 patients undergoing maximal CPX. ResultsBoth approaches showed similar prognostic accuracy, with sex-specific cut-offs. ConclusionsAbsolute and predicted OUES independently predicted mortality, supporting either approach for clinical risk stratification. Main PerspectiveCardiopulmonary exercise testing plays a central role in risk stratification for patients with heart failure, and the oxygen uptake efficiency slope (OUES) is a robust prognostic marker even when maximal effort is not achieved. In this study of more than 1,100 patients, absolute and age- and sex-adjusted OUES showed comparable accuracy for predicting mortality. We also identified sex-specific OUES thresholds, supporting a more individualized approach to prognostic assessment and clinical decision-making in heart failure.

papers.title: VectBox Sync: a web application for vectorcardiographic analysis of ventricular synchrony from 12-lead electrocardiograms
papers.abstract: We introduce VectBox Sync, a browser-based application that implements a published vectorcardiographic (VCG) dyssynchrony index for exploratory assessment of ventricular electrical synchrony from the 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG). Despite guideline-directed patient selection, a substantial fraction of patients who receive cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) do not obtain the expected benefit. QRS duration and morphology remain the principal electrical criteria, yet they do not capture the three-dimensional trajectory of ventricular activation. VectBox Sync prioritizes native digital ECG recordings, including matrices and common clinical and research waveform formats; optional manufacturer-PDF import and externally digitized numerical files extend access when paper-like archives are the only available source. After optional preprocessing, the user selects a QRS interval, and the application calculates the dyssynchrony index relative to a calibrated control cutoff. It also provides companion VCG descriptors (voltage and speed integrals, loop angles, and planarity), together with VCG trajectories, synchrony-field maps, and a multilingual PDF report. Labeled conditions from the same session can be overlaid for comparison, for example across successive pacing settings. VectBox Sync makes this VCG-based assessment accessible through an integrated web application, providing quantitative descriptors that complement conventional ECG criteria. The application is available at https://vectbox.com/sync for research and educational use.

papers.title: SGLT2 Inhibitors in Stage 5 Chronic Kidney Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Cardiovascular and Kidney Outcomes
papers.abstract: Evidence supporting SGLT2 inhibitor use in stage 5 chronic kidney disease remains limited because landmark trials have largely excluded this population. In this systematic review and meta-analysis, SGLT2 inhibitor use was associated with fewer heart failure hospitalizations and myocardial infarctions, while benefits for mortality and dialysis initiation remained uncertain. Dedicated randomized trials are needed to clarify their role in this population.

papers.title: Incidence of unruptured intracranial aneurysms: A nationwide population based longitudinal study
papers.abstract: BackgroundUnderstanding the epidemiology of unruptured intracranial aneurysm (UIAs) is crucial for risk stratification, clinical decision making, and public health planning. The aim of this study was to perform a nationwide population-based analysis to examine the incidence of unruptured intracranial aneurysms in Sweden. MethodsData were obtained from the Swedish National Patient Register for all persons, aged 18 years and older, diagnosed with an intracranial aneurysm (ICD-10: I67.1) between the years 2000 and 2020. Crude incidence was calculated for the total population and age- and gender-stratified groups. Age standardized incidence was assessed using the European standard population. The incidence of intracranial aneurysms diagnosed with concurrent subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) was also examined. ResultsDuring the study period, 8681 patients were diagnosed with UIA. The median age of diagnosis was 63 years and 65.1% were women. The age-standardized incidence increased approximately 74% % between 2000 and its peak: from 4.6 (95% CI: 4,26-4.95) per 100,000 in the year 2000 to 7.99 (95% CI: 6.7-7.54) per 100,000 in the year 2019. {square} The increase in incidence of UIAs was most pronounced among women and those aged above 60. During the study period, the number of cases with SAH decreased slightly. ConclusionsThe increasing incidence of UIAs in Sweden might be due improved clinical detection rates, demographic changes, and changes in the prevalence of risk factors. These findings highlight the importance of enhanced surveillance, effective risk stratification, and targeted public health strategies to address the growing burden of UIAs.

papers.title: Design and Validation of a Compact Sensor for Peripheral Pulse Waveform Capture
papers.abstract: Peripheral pulse waveforms captured across different sites of the vascular tree provide valuable insights into cardiovascular health. This study presents a low-cost compact sensor designed to minimize intrusion at the measurement site while capturing the pulse waveform. The sensor performance was characterized and evaluated through both in-vitro benchtop experiments and a pilot in-vivo clinical study against invasive arterial pressure waveforms. The proposed sensor was able to capture pulse waveform morphology with reliable beat to beat tracking. Although offsets were present in the calculated features, fundamental temporal trends and cardiac cycle profiles were preserved. Thus, this work lays the foundation for a scalable hardware platform capable of multi-site pulse monitoring, enabling its integration with emerging computational frameworks for cardiovascular risk screening.

papers.title: Gut microbiome and incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events in the general population: a prospective study in five European cohorts
papers.abstract: BackgroundAccumulating evidence suggests that the gut microbiota is implicated in cardiovascular disease. We investigated how the gut microbiome associates with incident major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), and cardiovascular and all-cause mortality (ACM) in a large, prospective, population-based study. The findings were tested for replication in four independent cohorts. MethodsGut microbiome composition was assessed via shallow shotgun sequencing in the FINRISK 2002 cohort, with up to 18 years of follow-up. Associations of microbial taxa with incident MACE were investigated using time-to-event analyses. Significant associated microbial features were tested for replication in four European cohorts (HUNT, HELIUS, SIMPLER, and SCAPIS) followed by a meta-analysis. ResultsIn the FINRISK 2002 cohort (1167 incident MACE events), nine taxa were significantly associated with incident MACE and sustained adjustments for traditional risk factors and multiple comparisons. The meta-analysis of replication cohorts (N=30,228; 1,938 participants with incident MACE) confirmed robust associations for several identified taxa. Specifically, higher abundance of genera Scardovia (HR=1.17 [95% CI 1.08-1.26], p= 0.0001) and Limosilactobacillus (HR=1.16 [95%CI 1.09-1.23], p= 1E-06) was associated with increased MACE risk, and increased risk of cardiovascular mortality and all-cause mortality. The species ER4 sp900317525 (HR=0.89 [95%CI 0.83-0.95], p=0.0005) was associated with lower hazard of MACE and all-cause mortality. ConclusionsThe gut metagenome showed robust associations with incident MACE, which were replicated in four independent European cohorts. Key microbial taxa also associated with incident MACE and mortality, suggesting their potential relevance as candidate risk markers for further studies. Clinical PerspectiveO_ST_ABSWhat is New?C_ST_ABSO_LIIn a large-scale discovery and replication study involving five European population-based cohorts (> 36,000 participants) we identified specific gut microbial taxa--including the genera Scardovia and Limosilactobacillus - which were significantly associated with increased risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). C_LIO_LIThe obligate anaerobic commensal ER4 sp900317525, member of the Oscillospiraceae family, was associated with a lower risk of incident MACE across independent cohorts. C_LIO_LIThese microbial signatures remained significant after adjusting for traditional cardiovascular risk factors and were further associated with both cardiovascular and all-cause mortality. C_LI What Are the Clinical Implications?O_LIThe gut microbiome may represent a novel and modifiable risk factor for MACE as well as cardiovascular- and all-cause mortality. C_LIO_LIThese findings provide a rationale for future clinical trials investigating whether targeted modulation of the gut microbiome--through diet, prebiotics, oral hygiene, or other targeted therapies--can reduce the risk of MACE and improve patient survival. C_LI

papers.title: CCL17-CCR4 Signalling Attenuates Pressure Overload-Induced Cardiac Remodelling Through IGFBP6 Suppression in Cardiac Fibroblasts
papers.abstract: Background and AimsChemokines are key regulators of immune-cell trafficking, inflammation, and tissue repair in cardiovascular disease. C-C motif chemokine ligand 17 (CCL17) has been linked to adverse remodelling after myocardial infarction and neurohumoral stress, but its function during sustained mechanical pressure overload is unknown. We investigated whether CCL17 regulates ventricular remodelling through cardiac fibroblast signalling. MethodsSerum proteomic screening and myocardial and serum validation were performed in patients with aortic stenosis and healthy controls. CCL17 function was evaluated using global Ccl17 deletion and adeno-associated virus-mediated CCL17 augmentation in mice subjected to transverse aortic constriction. Cardiac transcriptomics and complementary pharmacological, small interfering RNA, and promoter-reporter experiments in cardiac fibroblasts were used to define downstream signalling. Separately, fibroblast-directed Igfbp6 silencing was used to test the functional contribution of IGFBP6 in vivo. ResultsSerum CCL17 concentrations and myocardial CCL17 abundance were increased in patients with aortic stenosis, and cardiac and circulating CCL17 increased rapidly after transverse aortic constriction. Ccl17 deletion aggravated pressure overload-induced systolic dysfunction, hypertrophy, and fibrosis, whereas CCL17 augmentation conferred reciprocal protection. Transcriptomic analyses identified insulin-like growth factor-binding protein 6 (IGFBP6) as a CCL17-responsive candidate. In cardiac fibroblasts, CCL17 reduced secreted and cellular IGFBP6 and -smooth muscle actin through C-C chemokine receptor 4 (CCR4)-dependent signalling associated with suppression of early growth response 1 (EGR1). Genetic perturbation and promoter-reporter analyses further supported CCR4-EGR1-dependent regulation of Igfbp6. Finally, fibroblast-directed Igfbp6 silencing improved systolic function and reduced hypertrophy and fibrosis in Ccl17-deficient mice after transverse aortic constriction. ConclusionsOur findings identify CCL17 as a previously unrecognized cardioprotective factor and uncover a novel immune cell-fibroblast communication axis, whereby CCL17 restrains pressure overload-induced maladaptive cardiac remodelling through CCR4-EGR1-mediated suppression of IGFBP6 in cardiac fibroblasts. Graphical abstract O_FIG O_LINKSMALLFIG WIDTH=200 HEIGHT=82 SRC="FIGDIR/small/26367804v1_ufig1.gif" ALT="Figure 1"> View larger version (31K): org.highwire.dtl.DTLVardef@14e5facorg.highwire.dtl.DTLVardef@6b4a30org.highwire.dtl.DTLVardef@1d3bb7borg.highwire.dtl.DTLVardef@1b9ae1a_HPS_FORMAT_FIGEXP M_FIG C_FIG Pressure overload was associated with increased circulating and myocardial CCL17 in patients with aortic stenosis and mice subjected to transverse aortic constriction. In cardiac fibroblasts, CCL17 signals through CCR4 to suppress EGR1-dependent Igfbp6 transcription, thereby restraining fibroblast activation and extracellular matrix deposition. Accordingly, Ccl17 deficiency aggravated pressure overload-induced cardiac hypertrophy, fibrosis, and systolic dysfunction, whereas AAV-mediated CCL17 augmentation conferred reciprocal protection. Fibroblast-directed Igfbp6 silencing partially rescued the adverse remodelling phenotype in Ccl17-deficient mice. These findings identify CCL17 as an endogenous protective signal and establish the CCR4-EGR1-IGFBP6 pathway as a functionally relevant regulator of fibroblast activation during pressure overload.

papers.title: Effects of Sacred Dances versus Conventional Physical Training on Functional Capacity and Quality of Life in Women with Heart Failure: Protocol for a Randomized Active-Controlled Crossover Non-Inferiority Trial (RED-WHF)
papers.abstract: This protocol describes the RED-WHF trial, a randomized, active-controlled, two-period crossover clinical trial designed to evaluate whether Sacred Dances (SD)--as a mind-body intervention--are non-inferior to conventional physical training (PT) regarding functional capacity and quality of life in women with heart failure (HF). Sedentary behavior and emotional stress significantly worsen HF prognosis, yet conventional exercise programs face barriers in patient adherence and variable motivation. Sacred Dances, a form of low-to-moderate-intensity moving meditation, may enhance physical fitness while promoting emotional well-being and spiritual connection (flourishing). We will recruit 30 sedentary women aged 18 to 70 with stable HF (NYHA class I-III) and a documented left ventricular ejection fraction. Participants will be randomized 1:1 to one of two treatment sequences: SD followed by PT, or vice versa. Each 12-week intervention phase consists of two weekly sessions, lasting 90 minutes for SD (with 60 minutes of active dancing to allow choreography instruction) and 60 minutes for PT, separated by a 3-week washout period. Primary outcomes are functional capacity (6-minute walk test [6MWT]) and health-related quality of life (EQ-5D-5L Index and VAS). Secondary outcomes include adherence rates, spiritual attitudes (ARES scale), symptoms of depression, anxiety, and stress (DASS-21), and perceived subjective impact (EUPI-12). Statistical planning incorporates linear mixed models (LMM) with treatment, period, and sequence fixed effects, and an intention-to-treat approach with multiple imputation for missing data. To establish non-inferiority, a 30-meter margin for the 6MWT difference will be applied. The study was approved by the local Ethics Committee (CEP/EBMSP opinion 7.443.180, CAAE: 86133125.0.0000.5544) and prospectively registered in the Brazilian Registry of Clinical Trials (ReBEC ID: RBR-85tkdz5).

papers.title: Expert-level localization of fine-grained cardiac structures across the transthoracic echocardiogram
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence models for echocardiography interpret studies without identifying the structures that support their outputs. We show that this spatial grounding does not emerge from the pretraining of current vision-language models. General-purpose and medical vision-language models and an open- vocabulary detector recalled 3% or fewer of cardiac structures and scored below a box that never sees the image. EchoLens, a detector trained on 5,912 expert-annotated structures and 4,219 Doppler signals from 136 patients, recalled 87% and localized structures as reliably as a blinded expert reader (box centre within the reference in 95.7% and 95.3% of cases). It covers 21 structures across 11 transthoracic views and 11 spectral Doppler signal types. In external data, two physicians judged 81-92% of its detections correct across all 11 views, and it identified the Doppler signal type in 83% of frames. EchoLens provides the spatial layer that grounded echocardiographic interpretation requires.

papers.title: Cytokine Signatures of Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Myocarditis and the Modifying Role of Clonal Hematopoiesis: A Machine-Learning and Multi-Omics Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundImmune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) myocarditis affects up to 2% of patients on ICI and has up to a 50% mortality. Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential (CHIP) is a risk factor for ICI myocarditis. ObjectivesTo leverage a multi-omics approach to evaluate cytokines associated with ICI myocarditis, immunosuppression resistance, CHIP in ICI myocarditis and implicated pathways and cell type contributions. Methods236 cardio-oncology patients were enrolled, including 88 who were on ICI. Cytokine profiling from patients on ICI were sampled and analyzed using machine learning and explainable artificial intelligence. Single-cell multi-omics of peripheral blood from Yale (n=19), Stanford (n=25), and MGH (n=63) evaluated cell-type contributions of cytokines and implicated pathways. Validation of Yale proteomic analyses was done using the Stanford CYTOF dataset. ResultsTop features associated with ICI myocarditis included IL13, CXCL10, PDGF-A, CCL13, CCL17 and KITlg. Top KEGG pathways associated with ICI myocarditis and immunosuppression resistant ICI myocarditis included JAK-STAT signaling, IL17 signaling and lipid/atherosclerosis pathways. At the single-cell level, the consensus signals distinguishing myocarditis from non-myocarditis across cohorts was predominantly driven by module-level JAK-STAT, T-cell, and Toll-like receptor activation. Similar transcription gene programs were activated in CHIP carriers including modules implicated in the pro-inflammatory immune response, such as NF-kappa B, IL17, MAPK, and TNF pathways within CHIP cells spanning lymphoid (cytotoxic CD8+ NKT, and natural killer cells) and myeloid lineages. ConclusionsAcross cohorts, JAK-STAT signaling emerges as a convergent and potentially actionable axis in ICI myocarditis that is further amplified in CHIP carriers, supporting cytokine-guided risk stratification and JAK-STAT-directed immunosuppression as testable strategies.

papers.title: Nationwide Functional Profiling Enables Clinical Reclassification of KCNH2 Variants in the French LQT2 Population
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe increasing use of genetic testing has identified thousands of KCNH2 variants associated with long QT syndrome type 2 (LQT2), yet most remain variants of uncertain significance (VUS). Translating functional abnormalities into clinically actionable evidence remains a major challenge. We established a nationwide functional genomics strategy to systematically characterize KCNH2 variants identified in the French LQT2 population and improve their clinical interpretation. MethodsWe characterized 303 KCNH2 variants, including 201 VUS, using standardized high-throughput automated patch-clamp electrophysiology and complementary membrane trafficking assays. Nine electrophysiological parameters were integrated using MeTAL to predict variant-specific repolarization phenotypes under homozygous and heterozygous conditions. Modeled QTc values were compared with patient electrocardiographic data and variant-specific penetrance estimates. Functional evidence was calibrated against established benign and pathogenic variants using ClinGen-recommended categorical OddsPath and continuous likelihood-ratio approaches. ResultsMultidimensional functional profiling revealed abnormalities not captured by current amplitude alone, identifying additional variants with clinically relevant repolarization defects. Among variants assessed under heterozygous conditions, MeTAL predictions showed 82.9% concordance with patient QTc phenotypes for ACMG class 5 variants, with apparent discordances partly consistent with incomplete penetrance. Continuous likelihood-ratio calibration demonstrated strong discrimination between established benign and pathogenic variants (AUC=0.936) and provided graded functional evidence for 76.1% of VUS. Integration of calibrated functional evidence into the ACMG/AMP framework enabled reclassification of 64 of 201 VUS (31.8%), including 7 as pathogenic, 46 as likely pathogenic, and 11 as likely benign. ConclusionsThis nationwide study establishes a scalable framework integrating high-throughput electrophysiology, computational modeling, and clinical phenotyping to translate complex KCNH2 channel dysfunction into clinically interpretable evidence. The resulting reclassification of nearly one-third of VUS, together with the open-access HAMMER database, provides a resource to improve molecular diagnosis and risk assessment in LQT2.

papers.title: Beat-to-beat blood pressure variability and Alzheimers disease pathophysiology
papers.abstract: IntroductionElevated blood pressure variability (BPV) is predictive of Alzheimers disease neuropathologic change observed with AD biomarkers. However, prior studies have largely focused on visit-to-visit BPV, which may be influenced by antihypertensive medication adherence and other external factors. Few studies have investigated beat-to-beat BPV, a reliable and direct measure of cardiovascular and autonomic function relevant to AD. MethodsIndependently living older adults (N=132) were recruited from the community. Participants underwent continuous blood pressure monitoring and venipuncture. Plasma p- Tau217, p-Tau181, GFAP, NfL, and amyloid-{beta}42/40 ratio were assessed. Linear regression examined the relationship between beat-to-beat systolic BPV and plasma AD biomarkers with and without adjustment for age, sex, systolic blood pressure, and apolipoprotein E4 (APOE4) carrier status. ResultsElevated beat-to-beat BPV was associated with elevated plasma p-Tau217 ({beta}=0.32, p=0.008), plasma p-Tau181 ({beta}=0.22, p=0.05), and plasma GFAP ({beta}=0.41, p=0.00001). Elevated BPV was not associated with plasma amyloid-{beta}42/40 ratio or plasma NfL. DiscussionIncreased beat-to-beat BPV is associated with increased Core 1 T1 biomarkers of phosphorylated and secreted AD tau in blood plasma (i.e., pTau217, pTau181), but not with amyloid-{beta}42/40 ratio, a biomarker more exclusively indexing cerebral amyloid retention alone. Elevated BPV was also associated with higher plasma GFAP, a marker of astrocyte reactivity. These findings are consistent with prior studies relating visit-to-visit BPV to AD biomarkers, suggesting that intrinsic cardiovascular and/or autonomic factors underlie links between BPV and AD.

papers.title: Electromechanical Drivers of Diastolic Dysfunction During Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy Progression
papers.abstract: AimsDiastolic dysfunction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) reflects changes in sarcomeric function, electrophysiology, ventricular structure, and myocardial mechanics. Their effects on filling remain difficult to determine clinically. We sought to dissect these effects in MYH7-related non-obstructive HCM progression. MethodsWe developed a human biventricular electromechanical model linking electrophysiology and calcium handling to contraction, ventricular mechanics, haemodynamics, electrocardiography, and myocardial strain. Stage I represented MYH7 sarcomeric dysfunction before hypertrophy; Stage II added septal hypertrophy; Stage III added increased myocardial stiffness. Secondary ionic remodelling was examined at each stage and severity. ResultsSarcomeric dysfunction alone generated a low-volume hypercontractile phenotype before overt hypertrophy. Septal hypertrophy further constrained chamber filling, whereas myocardial stiffening exacerbated diastolic dysfunction and regional mechanical heterogeneity. Secondary ionic remodelling produced marked repolarisation abnormalities but, importantly, also prolonged calcium-tension dynamics and impaired relaxation, reducing ventricular filling to an extent comparable with structural remodelling in some disease states. Increasing ionic-remodelling severity progressively amplified these effects. Despite preserved ejection fraction (EF) throughout progression, ventricular volumes decreased while global and regional myocardial deformation deteriorated. ConclusionDiastolic dysfunction was evident before overt hypertrophy and worsened as structural, mechanical, and ionic abnormalities were added. Preserved EF did not reflect reduced ventricular filling or deterioration in myocardial strain. Regional mechanical measures may therefore reveal disease burden not captured by EF alone. By separating individual disease mechanisms, in silico modelling may help link measurable biomarkers to their underlying causes and support mechanism-based patient stratification. Our staged human biventricular electromechanical simulations suggest that sarcomeric dysfunction, septal hypertrophy, increased myocardial stiffness, and secondary ionic remodelling make distinct, yet interacting, contributions to diastolic impairment. Regional strain and active-stress measures may therefore reveal abnormalities that are not apparent from ejection fraction, while ECG and pressure-volume indices provide complementary information. Together, these markers could help distinguish underlying disease mechanisms and support more mechanistically informed patient stratification. C_FIG

papers.title: Screening Renin-Aldosterone Profiles and Long-term Cardiovascular Risk After Primary Aldosteronism Evaluation
papers.abstract: BackgroundAldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR) and plasma renin activity (PRA) are measured at the screening stage of primary aldosteronism (PA) evaluation, but their prognostic relevance after confirmatory classification and subsequent treatment remains uncertain. MethodsWe linked the seven-hospital Taiwan Primary Aldosteronism Investigation cohort (1991- 2023) with nationwide health insurance and mortality data through June 2025. Patients were classified as confirmatory-test-defined essential hypertension (EH), PA without adrenalectomy, or PA with subsequent adrenalectomy. Covariate-adjusted Cox models evaluated screening logARR, logPRA, and logPAC separately in relation to incident major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE; myocardial infarction, stroke, heart failure hospitalization, or cardiovascular death). ResultsAmong 3,178 participants (EH, 1,433; PA without adrenalectomy, 834; PA with adrenalectomy, 911), 441 (13.9%) experienced MACE during a median 7.9-year follow-up. Adjusted hazard ratios (95% CIs) per 1-unit increase in logARR were 1.09 (1.00-1.19), 1.14 (1.03-1.26), and 0.95 (0.87-1.05), respectively; corresponding logPRA estimates were 0.91 (0.83-0.99), 0.87 (0.79- 0.97), and 1.04 (0.93-1.16). LogPAC showed no consistent associations. Primary biomarker-by-phenotype interactions were not significant for logARR (P=0.057) or logPRA (P=0.069); time-varying adrenalectomy analyses were supportive but exploratory. ConclusionsHigher screening ARR and lower PRA were associated with subsequent MACE in confirmatory-test-defined EH and PA without adrenalectomy, but not clearly in PA with subsequent adrenalectomy.

papers.title: Trends in Cardiovascular Risk Factors, Disease Management, and Predicted Cardiovascular Risk Among US Adults, 1999-2023
papers.abstract: BackgroundCardiovascular risk factors have changed in the United States, but trends in prevalence, management, and predicted risk through the post-pandemic period remain incompletely characterized. MethodsWe analyzed 11 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) periods (1999-2000 through 2021-2023) among 60,199 nonpregnant adults aged [≥]20 years. Survey-weighted regression assessed age-standardized trends, subgroup differences, and measurement-change sensitivity. We assessed awareness, treatment, and control of hypertension, dyslipidemia, and diabetes. PREVENT equations estimated 10- and 30-year risks among adults without self-reported cardiovascular disease (CVD). ResultsObesity increased from 47.4% to 57.2% (odds ratio [OR] per decade, 1.23; 95% CI, 1.16-1.30), with class III obesity more than doubling (4.7% to 9.7%). Diabetes increased from 8.2% to 12.7% (OR, 1.26; 95% CI, 1.19-1.34), while current smoking declined from 24.4% to 14.9% (OR, 0.76; 95% CI, 0.71-0.81). Hypertension, dyslipidemia, chronic kidney disease, and prior CVD showed no significant linear trends, although mean systolic blood pressure (BP) (124.2 to 120.2 mm Hg) and total cholesterol (203.6 to 188.1 mg/dL) declined, alongside improvements in other lipids. Hypertension and dyslipidemia awareness and treatment increased, but BP control peaked at 32.5% in 2013-2014 before declining to 21.5%, while LDL cholesterol control rose from 17.0% to 34.2%. Diabetes awareness increased, but treatment trends were nonsignificant. Glycemic control peaked at 51.2% in 2003-2004 before declining to 41.9% (P for nonlinearity <0.001). Predicted 10-year total CVD risk declined from 5.66% to 5.28%; atherosclerotic CVD (ASCVD) risk declined by 0.16 percentage points per decade (95% CI, -0.22 to -0.09), while heart failure (HF) risk increased by 0.10 (95% CI, 0.03-0.17). Their 2021-2023 estimates were nearly identical (3.20% and 3.19%, respectively); 30-year risks showed similar divergence. ConclusionsImprovements in smoking, blood pressure, and lipids coexisted with rising obesity and diabetes, declining blood pressure control after earlier gains, and divergent predicted ASCVD and HF risks.

papers.title: Near-infrared spectroscopy reveals asymmetric hemispheric blood supply during aortic arch surgery
papers.abstract: ObjectivesBilateral and trilateral selective antegrade cerebral perfusion (SACP) aim to ensure symmetric hemispheric perfusion during aortic arch surgery, which current monitoring cannot directly assess. As a step towards real-time monitoring, we assessed the feasibility of multichannel contrast-enhanced near-infrared spectroscopy (CE-NIRS) using indocyanine green and whether hemispheric bolus timing matched expectations for each perfusion configuration. MethodsIn this prospective, offline-analysed pilot study, 10 patients undergoing aortic arch surgery (9 frozen elephant trunk) received 94 boluses across 10 perfusion configurations. The interhemispheric difference in time to peak ({Delta}TTP) was compared with the pre-bypass baseline using a linear mixed model with Holm correction, alongside cerebral oximetry; the relationship to postoperative cerebral injury was explored post hoc. Results92 of 94 boluses yielded a bilateral TTP. Contrary to expectation, the left hemisphere peaked later under bilateral (+7.2 s, 95% CI 3.4-11.0; p = 0.003) and trilateral SACP (+8.7 s, 2.5-14.8; p = 0.031). With both left-sided arch vessels on body perfusion, the asymmetry reversed (-7.0 s, -11.7 to -2.3; p = 0.025). {Delta}TTP detected 6 of 9 configuration effects, whereas oximetry detected none after correction. The three patients with cerebral injury showed the three most pronounced reversals (exact p = 0.100) but were also those managed trilaterally. ConclusionsMultichannel CE-NIRS is feasible during aortic arch surgery, without indicator-related adverse events. Bilateral and trilateral SACP did not secure symmetric indicator delivery; the configuration-dependent asymmetry and its reversal point to two steals within the perfusion circuit that oximetry missed. Their clinical relevance requires prospective confirmation.

papers.title: Provider-Level and Specialty Variation in ARNI and SGLT2i Use After Heart Failure Hospitalization
papers.abstract: BackgroundAngiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors (ARNI) and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) are incompletely utilized in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). The degree to which use varies at the individual level and within specialties is unknown. We aimed to characterize provider-level and specialty-level variation in ARNI and SGLT2i prescribing after HF hospitalization. MethodsThis retrospective cohort study included Veterans Affairs (VA) providers seeing patients within 6 months of HFrEF hospitalization 2017-2023. We used descriptive statistics and site-adjusted multilevel logistic regression to examine prescribing by medical specialty, provider type, and provider sex. Adjusted median odds ratios (mOR) and empirical (unadjusted) provider-level rate ratios (RRs) by percentile were used to describe provider-level variation. Clinical pharmacy visits were assessed as an independent factor and as an interaction with specialty. ResultsAmong 7,946 providers caring for 76,795 patients across 211,267 outpatient encounters, provider-level variation remained substantial after adjustment for patient characteristics and site-level clustering (mOR 1.45 for ARNI; 1.46 for SGLT2i). Within every specialty, providers ranged from near- zero to near-100% use. Relative to the median provider in the same specialty, RRs ranged from 0-0.31 (5th percentile), 0.37-0.71 (25th), 1.38-1.66 (75th), to 1.8-3.2 (95th). Cardiology visits carried the highest adjusted odds of ARNI (OR 2.30, 95% CI 2.18-2.44) and SGLT2i use (OR 1.99, 95% CI 1.88-2.11) and most new starts. Pharmacist visits were independently associated with greater use of ARNI (OR 1.14, 1.06-1.23) and SGLT2i (OR 1.15, 1.06-1.24), with no effect modification by specialty. In early 2023, 58.4% (ARNI) and 40.2% (SGLT2i) of post-hospitalization HF visits had untreated patients. ConclusionsProvider-level variation in ARNI and SGLT2i use after guideline incorporation was large within every specialty and independent of site effects. Though specific specialties have higher use, individual providers, not specialty alone, may be an important target for efforts to close gaps in therapy. CLINICAL PERSPECTIVEO_ST_ABSWhat Is New?C_ST_ABSO_LIIn the years following guideline incorporation, provider-level use of ARNI and SGLT2i after heart failure hospitalization ranged from near 0% to near 100% use within every specialty. Providers at the 95th percentile prescribed at 1.8 to 3.2 times the rate the median provider of the same specialty. C_LIO_LIProvider-level variation persisted after accounting for patient characteristics and site-level clustering (median odds ratios 1.45 for ARNI and 1.46 for SGLT2i) in a health system with a national formulary and low copayments. C_LI What Are the Clinical Implications?O_LIIndividual practice patterns within every specialty may be an important target for efforts to close gaps in guideline-directed therapy, and the drivers of this variation warrant study. C_LIO_LIVisits with cardiology and endocrinology providers were associated with greatest use of both medications, supporting specialty care for HF. Clinical pharmacists could play an important adjunctive role. C_LI

papers.title: Risk Factors for Progressive Cardiorenal Syndrome Events in Patients with Chronic Kidney Disease: The CRIC Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundCardiorenal syndrome (CRS) is associated with poor outcomes. Risk factors for progressive CRS are not understood in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). ObjectivesThis study aimed to determine the incidence of progressive CRS and risk factors in individuals with CKD. MethodsAdults with CKD in the Chronic Renal Insufficiency Cohort (CRIC) study excluding those with heart failure (HF) at baseline were included (n = 3,557). We defined progressive CRS as developing HF and end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) within 12 months. ESKD was defined as needing renal replacement therapy or renal transplant. The associations of baseline risk factors with progressive CRS were examined using Cox proportional hazards models. A sensitivity analysis assessed risk factors in those who developed HF before ESKD and vice versa. Results161 patients (4.5%) developed progressive CRS. Traditional risk factors [multivariable-adjusted hazard ratios (HR) (95% CI)] associated with progressive CRS in multivariable models included lower education [1.90 (1.28,2.83)], cardiovascular disease [1.53 (1.07,2.18)], lower estimated glomerular filtration rate [0.64 (0.51,0.82)] and higher albumin to creatinine ratio [2.44 (1.98,3.02)]. Novel risk factors associated included higher levels of alkaline phosphatase, brain natriuretic peptide (BNP), tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-), growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF-15), hemoglobin A1C, and lower hemoglobin. Risk factors associated with both ESKD before HF and HF before ESKD were kidney dysfunction, albuminuria, and mineral bone disorder (higher alkaline phosphatase and PTH), inflammation (TNF-), fibrotic factor (GDF-15), and anemia. Diabetes, CVD, systolic blood pressure, waist circumference, HbA1c, and BNP were more strongly associated when HF preceded ESKD. ConclusionsBoth traditional risk factors and novel risk factors associated with inflammation, mineral bone disorder, anemia, diabetes control, albuminuria, worse kidney function, and fibrotic factors are associated with progressive CRS in individuals with CKD. Many of these risk factors are modifiable representing potential areas for intervention.

papers.title: A Behaviorally Informed Patient-Facing Intervention to Promote Albuminuria Testing in Hypertension: A Mixed-Methods Evaluation of KnowCKD
papers.abstract: BackgroundAlbuminuria testing to diagnose chronic kidney disease (CKD) and guide blood pressure management is recommended for adults with hypertension but remains underused in part due to suboptimal patient understanding of its importance. Patient-facing behavioral interventions have the potential to bridge this gap. We developed and evaluated KnowCKD, a behaviorally informed intervention designed to increase patient awareness of CKD and knowledge and promote albuminuria testing among adults with hypertension. MethodsKnowCKD consisted of an educational infographic and brief, behaviorally informed messages delivered to patients smartphones during the 5 days leading up to and including a scheduled primary care visit at one academic medical center. Among 57 adults with hypertension without diabetes or recent albuminuria testing, we assessed changes in CKD awareness and knowledge and patient-reported engagement via survey pre- and post-exposure to KnowCKD. Electronic Health Record (EHR)-confirmed albuminuria or proteinuria testing was compared with 182 contemporaneous primary care controls using unmatched and propensity score-matched analysis. A post-intervention focus group evaluated participant experiences. ResultsAfter exposure to KnowCKD, recognition that adults with hypertension should undergo urine testing increased from 58% to 95%, knowledge that albuminuria indicates protein in the urine increased from 47% to 95%, and awareness that testing facilitates early CKD detection increased from 55% to 100% (P <0.001 for all). After the primary care visit, 77% of patients reported asking their clinician about urine testing and 65% reported that testing was ordered. EHR-confirmed albuminuria or proteinuria testing occurred in 36.8% of KnowCKD participants versus 11.0% of controls (risk ratio, 3.35 [95% CI, 1.96-5.73]; absolute risk difference, 25.9 percentage points [95% CI, 12.5-39.2]). The propensity score-matched risk ratio was 2.93 (95% CI, 1.59-5.42). Participants described KnowCKD as timely, understandable, and actionable and emphasized trusted health-system communication for broader implementation. ConclusionsKnowCKD was associated with increased patient awareness of CKD and knowledge, patient engagement, and higher EHR-confirmed albuminuria or proteinuria testing among adults with hypertension. A rigorous evaluation of KnowCKD implementation within routine health-system workflows is warranted as a next step.

papers.title: Single-cell profiling of human plaques reveals cellular and molecular signatures of symptomatic atherosclerosis
papers.abstract: Atherosclerotic plaque vulnerability drives ischemic cardiovascular events, yet the cellular and molecular signatures distinguishing symptomatic from asymptomatic human plaques remain poorly defined. Here, we compared 53 symptomatic and asymptomatic human carotid plaques using single-nucleus (snRNA-seq; 17 samples, 19,100 nuclei; AtherOMICS biobank) and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq; 36 samples, 68,983 cells; four public datasets), analysed independently and combined by meta-analysis. Across sequencing approaches, symptomatic plaques showed cell-state shifts toward later or terminal states in osteochondrogenic smooth muscle cells (SMCs) and CD4 T cells, as well as transcriptional changes toward inflammatory and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in endothelial cells (ECs), T cells, and fibroblasts. Nuclear profiling uncovered a depletion of fibroblasts in symptomatic plaques, marked by downregulation of RGS5. Integrating these transcriptomic signatures with genome-wide association data for coronary, cerebrovascular, and peripheral atherosclerotic disease, we found that genetic risk was enriched primarily in vascular wall cells (SMCs, fibroblasts, ECs), rather than immune cell types. The analyses further nominated higher TWIST1 expression in ECs (colocalized with risk across four atherosclerotic phenotypes), lower GUCY1A1 expression in fibroblasts and macrophages, and higher MRAS expression in T cells as candidate driver mechanisms linking genetic risk to symptomatic plaque transition. These findings provide novel insights into cellular and molecular phenotypes associated with plaque vulnerability and identify potential driver mechanisms of symptomatic plaque transformation that could inform therapeutic development.

papers.title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists Added to Statin Therapy and Cardiovascular Outcomes in ASCVD A Propensity Score-Matched Cohort Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundAdding a GLP-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) to statin therapy in patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) and obesity may reduce cardiovascular risk, yet real-world evidence is limited. ObjectivesTo evaluate whether GLP-1 RA use added to statins is associated with lower all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction (MI), and ischemic stroke versus statin monotherapy in ASCVD patients with body mass index (BMI) [≥]30 kg/m2. MethodsUsing the TriNetX Research Network (108 U.S. healthcare organizations), we identified ASCVD patients with BMI [≥]30 kg/m2 on statins initiating a GLP-1 RA (n=166,278) versus statin-only controls (n=920,176). Propensity score matching on 34 covariates yielded 119,911 matched pairs followed [≤]3 years. Prespecified analyses included a BMI [≥]35 subgroup (62,385 pairs), four washout sensitivity analyses (30-120 days), and a familial hypercholesterolemia exclusion analysis (161,312 matched pairs).
